strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Exfiltration Over C2 Channel

analytics.name: Analytic 0988
analytics.guidance: Identifies suspicious outbound traffic volume mismatches from processes that typically do not generate network activity, particularly over C2 protocols like HTTPS, DNS, or custom TCP/UDP ports, following file or data access.

tuning.description: Set threshold for outbound transfer size exceeding typical C2 traffic (e.g., >1MB in <5min).
List of approved processes that may exhibit high outbound traffic (e.g., updates).

analytics.name: Analytic 0989
analytics.guidance: Monitors for processes reading sensitive files then immediately initiating unusual outbound connections or bulk transfer sessions over persistent sockets, particularly with encrypted or binary payloads.

tuning.description: Threshold for high-entropy payloads indicative of encoded or encrypted exfil data.
Defines length of time over which transfer size must be aggregated to trigger detection.

analytics.name: Analytic 0990
analytics.guidance: Detects unauthorized applications or scripts accessing sensitive data followed by establishing encrypted outbound communication to rare external destinations or with abnormal byte ratios.

tuning.description: Enables defenders to tune legitimate vs. suspicious lineage (e.g., launchd → curl is uncommon).
Focus detection on unusual protocols (e.g., IRC, FTP, DNS over HTTPS).

analytics.name: Analytic 0991
analytics.guidance: Detects VMs sending outbound traffic through non-standard services or to unknown destinations. Exfiltration over reverse shells tunneled via VMkernel or custom payloads routed via hostd/vpxa.

tuning.description: Limit detection to sensitive or externally-exposed VMs handling confidential data.
Minimum outbound transfer size before flagging anomalous C2-based exfiltration.
Define expected protocols for outbound data (e.g., disallow FTP/SCP over high ports).

mitigations.name: Network Intrusion Prevention
mitigations.description: Network intrusion detection and prevention systems that use network signatures to identify traffic for specific adversary malware can be used to mitigate activity at the network level. Signatures are often for unique indicators within protocols and may be based on the specific obfuscation technique used by a particular adversary or tool, and will likely be different across various malware families and versions. Adversaries will likely change tool command and control signatures over time or construct protocols in such a way to avoid detection by common defensive tools. (Citation: University of Birmingham C2)
